title: Vaisakhi and the first share
hookLine: the wheat turns gold, and before anyone eats the new grain, the first of it goes back
carry: food is a gift; the first share goes back
tomorrow: where did Sita go when Ram sent her away?

cards: Months after the Lohri fire, the fields have changed color. The wheat planted in the cold stands gold and heavy, and the sickles are coming out.
In the villages there's a fair: drums, swings, sugarcane, young men dancing bhangra with their arms up as if lifting the whole harvest. The day is Vaisakhi.
And in Hindu homes there's a rule older than any fair: before anyone eats, the first share goes back. Today, where that rule comes from: a story Krishna tells about the very beginning.

teach.h: VAISAKHI: HARVEST AND A NEW YEAR
teach.b: Vaisakhi takes its name from the spring month of Vaishakh. For Hindus in Punjab it's the harvest, and a new year by the sun.
Some families bathe at dawn in a river or a temple tank, then take the first of the grain to the temple. Why the first?
Picture the Bhagavad Gita's battlefield: two armies waiting, and Arjuna asking why he should act at all. Krishna answers by telling how things began.
In paraphrase: when the Creator made human beings, he made them together with yajna, sacrifice, the giving back, and said: grow by this. Care for the gods, and they will care for you.
From yajna comes rain, from rain comes grain. Then Krishna says something blunt.

Whoever enjoys the gifts without giving anything back is a thief. The good eat what remains after the offering; those who cook only for themselves, he says, eat their own wrong. That's the teaching under a Hindu harvest.

It's given, by the earth, the rain and God, and the first share goes back. It's why so many Hindu families set a plate before the shrine before anyone eats, and why what comes back is called prasad, a gift.
On Vaisakhi it's why the first grain goes to the temple and to those who have less. The same street keeps another Vaisakhi too.
For Sikhs, it remembers Guru Gobind Singh founding the Khalsa, told in their own words, and their langar feeds anyone who walks in.

teach.h: AN OPEN HAND, BOTH SIDES OF THE STREET.
teach.b: Two traditions, two reasons, and at harvest, an open hand on both sides of the street.

how: Hindus in Punjab keep Vaisakhi as the harvest and the solar new year, some bathing in a sacred river or temple tank at dawn, offering the first of the grain at the temple and giving to others; at home, food is offered before the shrine before anyone eats.

games.why: the Gita says the good eat what remains after the offering. food is a gift, so the first share goes back.

practice: Picture tonight's plate in front of you. Before your hand reaches for it, pause. If you pray, offer it first, silently or with a word, to God or to Krishna, and let what comes back be prasad.
If you don't pray, take one breath for where it came from: the field, the rain, the hands that grew and cooked it. Rest in that pause now, so it's ready at dinner.
